passage: The night before the test, Rajni opened the Civics chapter and closed it again. "So boring," she told her friend Amandeep on the phone. "Ma'am never asks from it." "It might come," said Amandeep. "It won't," said Rajni. She spent the hour on the chapters she liked, and went to bed early. In the exam hall, the last page had a question worth eight marks. It was from Civics. She read it twice and wrote two lines, then stared at the clock. When the paper was returned, she had lost most of those marks, and they were the easy ones.

qa.q: How many marks was the Civics question worth?
What was Rajni feeling when she saw the eight-mark Civics question?
qa.a: She felt shocked and uneasy. She read it twice, wrote only two lines and stared at the clock.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Rajni use for a chapter she dislikes, and why?
qa.a: She could read the chapter in short bursts, picking out the main points first. Then even a boring chapter would not leave big gaps.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see what happened in the exam?
qa.a: Amandeep warned Rajni that it might come, and it did. Amandeep may feel sorry for Rajni but also that the hint was ignored.

grounding: A girl skips the Civics chapter she dislikes and hopes it will not come, but the paper has an eight-mark question on it and she loses easy marks.

passage:
"Aren't you reading Civics?" Siddharth asked, peeling a banana.
"Local government? Boring. Ma'am never asks from the last chapter anyway."
"She might."
"She won't. I'm doing History twice instead."
Next evening Swati came home and dropped her bag.
"How was it?"
"There was a question on the panchayat. Eight marks. The whole thing."
"The chapter you skipped?"
"Don't." She pulled at her plait. "It was easy. I read the first page once, weeks ago. I could only write two lines."
Siddharth sat down next to her. "So... next time?"
"Next time I read the boring one first."

qa.q: How many marks was the question on the panchayat worth?
How did Swati feel when she came home after the test?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and annoyed with herself, pulling at her plait, because the question was easy and she could only write two lines.

qa.q: What would have been a better way to handle the boring chapter?
qa.a: Read it first while fresh, or at least make short notes; betting that Ma'am wouldn't ask from it cost her eight easy marks.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see the result?
qa.a: Siddharth had warned 'She might', but he doesn't gloat; he sits beside her and gently asks about next time.

grounding: Shows a girl skipping a disliked Civics chapter on the guess it won't be asked, then losing easy marks on an eight-mark question.

subtype: Approach: skipping the boring chapter and hoping it will not come [Pitfall]
passage: In Class 7, I decided Civics was a waste of my time. The chapter on the Constitution was all long words, and my friend Farida said, 'Sir never asks from Civics in the half-yearly.' So I skipped it completely and did Geography maps instead. My mother's 'Sudha beti, read everything' went in one ear and out the other. On exam day I turned the paper over and there it was: Question 5, eight marks, 'Explain any four Fundamental Rights.' Farida groaned beside me. I knew they were in the book, on one easy page with a picture, but I had never looked. I left half the space empty. When the papers came back, Sir said, 'Sudha, those were your easiest eight marks.'

qa.a: 'Explain any four Fundamental Rights', for eight marks.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when Sir said those were the easiest eight marks?
qa.a: Sudha probably felt regret and embarrassment, knowing the answer was on one easy page Sudha had never looked at.

qa.q: What would you change first in Sudha's preparation?
qa.a: Read every chapter at least once, starting with the disliked one; relying on Farida's guess cost her easy marks.

qa.q: How might Farida feel about her own advice?
qa.a: Farida groaned at Question 5, so Farida may have felt guilty for saying Sir never asks from Civics.

grounding: Illustrates a girl leaving out the Civics chapter she dislikes, betting it won't be asked, and losing an easy eight-mark question.
